title: Session 1: Python Basics
text: Today’s learning goals · Be able to read and write short Python programs (using variables, lists, loops, conditionals, and functions) which is genuinely all the Python an experiment needs.

title: Session 1: Python Basics
text:
Learning outcomes
After this session, you can:

Work in the Python environment on UCloud: open it, write code, run it, and read what the output (including error messages) tells you.
Create and inspect variables of different types, manipulate strings (.split(), .upper(), len()), format output with f-strings, and compare values (==, !=, <, >).
Build and modify lists: index, slice, append, remove, replace, and sort.
Write for loops to repeat an action over a list (i.e., the exact shape of an experiment’s trial loop (for each image: show it, record a response, give feedback)).
Use conditionals (if / elif / else) to make code respond differently to different inputs, including inside loops.
Define your own functions with parameters and return values: the tool that lets you write “show a stimulus, collect a response” once and call it 200 times.

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment
text:
Python Coder in UCloud
Today we will learn the fundamentals of Python in UCloud, where Python is already installed. This gives everyone a consistent setup and lets us focus on the language itself instead of troubleshooting software installation or technical setup.
Next week, when you use PsychoPy, you will install it on your laptop and work with the version of Python bundled with it. We start with plain Python first so you can build a solid foundation before adding the extra complexity of PsychoPy.

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment

text:
How to open Python Coder in UCloud

Open UCloud.
Go to your E26_LICS_Methods1 workspace using the drop-down menu in the top-left corner.
Open the Applications page by clicking the shopping bag icon in the right panel.
Search for “Coder” and click the application.
The Job Parameters page should open. Fill in the fields the same way you do for your RStudio jobs:

Choose a meaningful job name
Select the machine type (only one option is available)
Click “Add Folder #1” and choose your cogsci_methods01_e26 folder
Under “Initialization”, select the ucloud_init_env_final.sh script
Choose a reasonable number of hours

Click the green “Submit” button.
When the job is ready, click “Open Interface” at the top left.

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment
text:
Install the Python language extension
Remember that we need to reinstall packages in UCloud every time we start a new job, because each job is assigned to a new remote computer. The same is true for Python: we need to install the Python language extension in the Coder application each time we start a new job. Here’s how:

In the far-left panel, click the icon with four squares. This is the marketplace icon.
Type “Python” into the search bar. The Python extension should be at the top of the list (from ms-Python).
Click the Python extension, then click the Install button.

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment
section: Create your first Python code file
text:
Create your first Python code file
You can now create a new Python code file. Here’s how:

In the far-left panel, find the icon that looks like three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other. Click it.
A pop-up menu will appear. Click File > New File.
A drop-down menu will appear asking for the file type. Type “Python” and you should see: Create new file (python) Built-in.
You will be prompted to choose where to save the file. For now, we will use: /work/cogsci_methods01_e26/name_of_your_file.py

You can choose any name for the file (it does not have to be “name_of_your_file.py”). The only rules are that you cannot use spaces and it must have a .py extension, because this tells the remote computer that it is a Python file when you reopen it later.

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment
section: “Hello world!”: Run your first line of Python code
text:
“Hello world!”: Run your first line of Python code
In your new code file, enter your first line of Python code:
print("Hello world!")

Your first prediction! Throughout these sessions, boxes like this ask you to guess what code will do before you run it. That’s where the learning happens, and wrong guesses are very welcome and encouraged. After a few tries the box will offer to show you the answer, so you can never get stuck. So: what exactly will appear in the console when this line runs? Take a guess.

Hello world!. Note that there are no quotation marks. The quotes tell Python where the text starts and ends; they are not part of the text itself.


Now run the code by highlighting it and pressing Shift+Enter. You should see a dedicated terminal open below.
Terminal shows what you expected? Next: Chapter 2 — Variables and types.

title: 3 · Loops
text: Block 3 · Learning goals: Understand basic for and while loops.

title: 3 · Loops
text:
What is a loop?
A loop is a programming structure that repeats a block of code.
In this lesson, you will meet two common types of loop:

For loops repeat code once for each item in a collection, such as a list.
While loops repeat code while a condition is true.







Basic for loops





For loops repeat the same code once for each item in a collection, such as a list.
Imagine that you have five subject IDs and want to print each one.
You could write a separate print() statement for every subject:
print("S01")
print("S02")
...
print("S05")
However, this becomes repetitive and difficult to update. Instead, store the IDs in a list and loop through the items:
subject_ids = ['S01', 'S02', 'S03', 'S04', 'S05']

for subject in subject_ids:
    print(subject)
In plain language, this loop means:

For every item in subject_ids, store that item in subject and print it.

The indented line is the body of the loop: it runs once per item. Each repetition is called an iteration. During each iteration, subject temporarily holds the current ID.
You can also loop through the index positions in a list. This is useful when you need both an item’s position and its value.
Notice the syntax: the for statement ends with a colon, and the loop body must be indented.

# Get the total number of subjects.
number_of_subjects = len(subject_ids)

# Create indices from 0 up to, but not including, number_of_subjects.
subject_index_range = range(number_of_subjects)

# Use each index to retrieve the corresponding subject ID.
for index in subject_index_range:
    print(f"Subject {index + 1}: {subject_ids[index]}")

Sometimes you need to update a number on every iteration of a loop.
This number is called a counter variable. The example below counts how many days have been processed.

# Define a list to loop over.
weekdays = ['monday', 'tuesday', 'wednesday', 'thursday', 'friday', 'saturday', 'sunday']

# Start a counter at zero.
day_of_week = 0

# Print each day, then add 1 to the counter.
for day in weekdays:
    print(f"The current day is {day}")
    day_of_week += 1

# Print the final count after the loop has finished.
print(f"There are {day_of_week} days in the list.")









Basic while loops





While loops repeat a block of code while a condition is True.
You will learn more about conditions after the logical-operators lesson. For now, this example prints the first six weekdays:

# Start at the first item in the list.
day_of_week = 0

# Keep looping while day_of_week is less than 6.
while day_of_week < 6:
    print(f"The current day is {weekdays[day_of_week]}")
    # Move to the next index so the condition will eventually become False.
    day_of_week += 1
The condition is day_of_week < 6. On each iteration, day_of_week increases by 1. Once it reaches 6, the condition is False and the loop stops.









Summary



Loops repeat code. Use a for loop when you want to work through each item in a collection, such as a list of subject IDs. Use an index-based for loop when you also need each item’s position. A counter variable records progress by changing on every iteration. Use a while loop when repetition should continue only while a condition is True.

title: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait
text:
Block 2 · aim to have Exercise 4 running by lunch (~12:00)
The wonderful thing about the draw-flip cycle is that every stimulus type follows it. Images work exactly like text: swap TextStim for ImageStim:
crumbs: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait

title: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait
text:
Two ways to wait
After a flip, we decide how long the stimulus stays. There are two fundamentally different answers, and choosing between them is an experimental design decision:
core.wait(2)        # the COMPUTER decides: exactly 2 seconds
event.waitKeys()    # the PARTICIPANT decides: waits for a key press






🔮 Predict first — which wait for which screen?



For each screen, decide: core.wait() or event.waitKeys()?

an instructions screen · (b) a feedback screen after a response · (c) a brief fixation cross between trials · (d) a word in a self-paced reading experiment







Check your prediction






waitKeys(): people read at different speeds. (b) wait(): fixed, comparable duration for everyone. (c) wait(): fixed and short. (d) waitKeys(): the whole point of self-paced reading is that the participant controls the pace; the time they take is the measurement. More on that in Session 3.
crumbs: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait

title: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait
text:
Try it
Modify your Chapter 3 script: after the Hello, world! screen, show one CogWheel image (pick any file from stimuli/), participant-paced. Run it.






Show the code





from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), color='black')

text = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hello, world!',
                       color='white', height=0.1)
text.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

img = visual.ImageStim(win, image='stimuli/stimulus1_L.jpg')
img.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

win.close()
core.quit()
Note the pattern repeating: prepare, draw, flip, wait — once per screen.
crumbs: 4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait

title: 6 · Exercise 4: Display the CogWheel Stimuli
text:
Block 2 milestone · this is the “running by lunch” target



Hands-on · work in pairs · swap driver/navigator halfway


Exercise 4 — Display the CogWheel stimuli


Your first real experiment script: show every stimulus image, one by one, participant-paced.



🎬 What success looks like: (embed a 10-second screen recording here: welcome text → a few cogwheel images advancing on key presses → goodbye text) — your goal is to make your screen do exactly this.

Build it in five steps, running your script after every step. Try each step yourself first; the folded code is there when you need it.

Step 1 — Collect the stimuli
Start a new script cogwheel.py in the workshop folder. Import what you need and collect the image files into a list. Print it to check.






Show the code





from psychopy import visual, event, core
import glob

images = glob.glob('stimuli/stimulus*.jpg')
print(images)   # sanity check: a list of file paths





Step 2 — Open the window
A window with a black background. Keep fullscr=False until everything works, then switch it on.






Show the code





win = visual.Window(fullscr=True, color='black')





Step 3 — Welcome the participant
A welcome message in white text; wait for a key press before starting. Remember: prepare, draw, flip, wait.






Show the code





welcome = visual.TextStim(win,
    text='Welcome to the CogWheel experiment!\n\nPress any key to begin.',
    color='white')
welcome.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()





Step 4 — The trial loop
Loop over the images: for each one, create an ImageStim, draw, flip, wait for a key press.






Show the code





for image in images:
    stim = visual.ImageStim(win, image=image)
    stim.draw()
    win.flip()
    event.waitKeys()





Step 5 — Goodbye and shutdown
After the loop: a goodbye message for two seconds, then close and quit.






Show the code





goodbye = visual.TextStim(win,
    text='That was it — thank you!', color='white')
goodbye.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(2)

win.close()
core.quit()









Stuck? The usual suspects




Empty list from glob → path problem; your script is not next to stimuli/.
Blank screen in the loop → missing win.flip(), or a draw() outside the loop.
Only one image ever shows → indentation: is everything that belongs to a trial inside the loop?

Ten minutes stuck? → partner → checkpoint below → red sticky.


Finished early? Add a fixation cross (visual.TextStim(win, text='+')) shown for half a second between images, or count trials with a variable and show the count in the goodbye message.






Checkpoint · complete Exercise 4 script





from psychopy import visual, event, core
import glob

# --- setup ---
images = glob.glob('stimuli/stimulus*.jpg')

win = visual.Window(fullscr=True, color='black')

# --- welcome screen ---
welcome = visual.TextStim(win,
    text='Welcome to the CogWheel experiment!\n\nPress any key to begin.',
    color='white')
welcome.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

# --- trial loop ---
for image in images:
    stim = visual.ImageStim(win, image=image)
    stim.draw()
    win.flip()
    event.waitKeys()

# --- goodbye and shutdown ---
goodbye = visual.TextStim(win,
    text='That was it — thank you!', color='white')
goodbye.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(2)

win.close()
core.quit()
Keep this script safe. Block 4 upgrades it, and Session 3 extends it into your Portfolio 2 prototype.

title: 2 · Meet PsychoPy: Three Modules and a Window
text:
Block 1 · aim to finish chapters 1–3 by the first break (~10:30)
Experiments need a screen: stimuli to look at, keys to press, precise timing. This is what PsychoPy adds. PsychoPy is a free, open-source Python library for behavioural experiments, made by psychologists for psychologists (Peirce, 2007). It is not a new language — it is a set of tools we import into the Python you already know. And because you are using the Standalone PsychoPy app, everything is already installed: the Coder runs your scripts in PsychoPy’s own bundled Python.
Three modules do almost everything we need today:
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
2 · Meet PsychoPy: Three Modules and a Window

title: 2 · Meet PsychoPy: Three Modules and a Window
text:
Your first window
Type this into a new script — call it my_first_window.py — and run it:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(
1    size=(1280, 720),
2    color='black',
3    fullscr=False)

core.wait(2)
win.close()
core.quit()

1

Width and height in pixels.

2

Background colour — try 'grey' or 'white' later.

3

Keep False while developing; switch to True for the real experiment.


A black window appears for two seconds, then closes. Not exciting yet — but note that win is just a variable, like any Python object from Session 1, and it has functions attached: win.flip(), win.close().






The escape hatch (you will need it today)



Sooner or later a window will freeze on you. It happens to everyone. Click on the console and press Ctrl-C (or close the window via the taskbar). This is exactly why we develop with fullscr=False: a small window is much easier to escape.








Checkpoint · end of Chapter 2





Your my_first_window.py should look like this and run without errors:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(
    size=(1280, 720),
    color='black',
    fullscr=False)

core.wait(2)
win.close()
core.quit()
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
2 · Meet PsychoPy: Three Modules and a Window

title: 3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Block 1 · aim to finish chapters 1–3 by the first break (~10:30)
Here is the single most important mechanic of the day. PsychoPy uses double buffering: there are two screen buffers, and you never draw directly onto the visible one. Showing a stimulus always takes three steps:
Think of a theatre: the back buffer is backstage, the front buffer is the stage. You can arrange the whole scene backstage. Draw as many stimuli as you like, and flip() raises the curtain in a single instant.
Why this design? A typical monitor redraws 60 times per second, so one frame lasts ~16.7 ms. Because the swap happens between two refreshes, stimulus onset is a single, well-defined moment: the moment of the flip. In Session 3 we will reset a clock at exactly that moment to measure reaction times.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)

title: 3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Hello, world, the full cycle
Type and run:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), color='black')

text = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hello, world!',
                       color='white', height=0.1)
text.draw()      # paint it backstage
win.flip()       # curtain up!

event.waitKeys() # pause until any key is pressed

win.close()      # close the window
core.quit()      # end the session cleanly
You should see Hello, world! in white on black, staying until you press a key.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)

title: 3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
The sabotage lab
Now break it on purpose — three times. This is not busywork: each sabotage teaches you to recognise one of today’s three most common bugs before it happens to you by accident.






🔮 Sabotage 1, predict first



Delete the line win.flip(). What will you see when you run it?






Check your prediction





A blank black window. The text was drawn — but only to the back buffer, which was never swapped to the screen. Blank screen almost always means a missing flip.











🔮 Sabotage 2, predict first



Put win.flip() back. Now delete event.waitKeys(). What happens?






Check your prediction





The text flashes for a split second and vanishes. The script runs straight to the end, and closing the window takes the text with it. Every flip needs a waiting step after it, or the participant sees almost nothing.











🔮 Sabotage 3, predict first



Restore everything. Now delete the last two lines (win.close() and core.quit()). What happens after you press a key?






Check your prediction





The script ends, but the window lingers as a frozen grey zombie. Always shut down cleanly — and now you know what a zombie window means when you see one.





Repair your script so all three sabotages are undone. Say the mantra once, prepare, draw, flip, wait, and take a break if the clock says so.






Checkpoint · end of Block 1





from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), color='black')

text = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hello, world!',
                       color='white', height=0.1)
text.draw()
win.flip()

event.waitKeys()

win.close()
core.quit()
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
3 · The Draw–Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)

title: 5 · Let Python Find Your Stimuli
text:
Block 2 · aim to have Exercise 4 running by lunch (~12:00)

Our experiment has many stimulus images. We could type every filename into a list by hand. This is fragile: one typo crashes the script, and adding stimuli means editing code. Instead, let Python find the files:
import glob

images = glob.glob('stimuli/stimulus*.jpg')
print(images)
The * is a wildcard that matches anything, so the pattern collects every file in stimuli/ whose name starts with stimulus and ends with .jpg.






🔮 Predict first



Before running: what type of thing will print(images) show? And what would glob.glob('stimuli/*_L.jpg') give you instead?






Check your prediction





A plain Python list of strings (file paths) — which means everything from Session 1 works on it: len(images), images[0], for image in images:. The second pattern collects only the left-response stimuli — wildcards can sit anywhere in the pattern.





Run it and look at the output. If the list is empty, stop and fix that now (it is a path problem, see Chapter 4). Every later chapter depends on this line working.






Good to know



glob does not guarantee any particular file order. For us that is fine. We shuffle in Chapter 7 anyway. If you ever need a fixed order, wrap it: sorted(glob.glob(...)).

title: 11 · From Cogwheels to Words
text:
Block 4 · the wrap-up. Read this even if you are behind
Step back and admire your script: it opens a window, presents randomised stimuli, restricts and records responses, evaluates them against a rule, and gives feedback. That is a genuine behavioural experiment, and its skeleton (setup → trial loop → shutdown) is shared by essentially every paradigm in cognitive science.
Now, CogComm asks how people process language in real time. So consider a thought experiment: what if the stimulus were not a cogwheel image but a word — and the measure were not accuracy, but how long you look at the word before pressing on? If a word is surprising or hard to process, you slow down, and your experiment can see it. That paradigm is called self-paced reading, and here is the punchline: your Exercise 5 script is already about 80% of it.

title: 11 · From Cogwheels to Words
text:
Before next session

Finish Exercise 5 if you did not get all the way, and keep both scripts safe: Session 3 extends them directly into the Portfolio 2 prototype.
Re-run your script and change one thing on purpose (a colour, a key, the feedback duration). Predict what will happen before you run it.
Optionally, skim the PsychoPy chapters of the Programming Experiments in Python and PsychoPy3 gitbook, and keep psychopy.org and learnpython.org bookmarked.
Bring questions — broken scripts very welcome.

Say it once more with feeling: prepare, draw, flip, wait. See you in Session 3.

title: 1 · Warming Up: A Python Refresher
text:
Block 1 · aim to finish chapters 1–3 by the first break (~10:30)

Let’s warm up the Python muscles from Session 1. Everything you learned there — variables, lists, loops, conditionals, functions — gets used today.






🔮 Predict first



Read this snippet and write down (yes, actually write down) exactly what it will print, line by line — before running it.
words = ['tea', 'coffee', 'water', 'juice']
words.append('cocoa')

for w in words:
    if len(w) > 5:
        print(w.upper())
    else:
        print(w)


Now type it into the Coder and run it.






Check your prediction





It prints:
tea
COFFEE
water
juice
cocoa
Only 'coffee' has more than 5 letters, so only it is uppercased. Two classic traps: forgetting that .append() added 'cocoa' before the loop started, and thinking 'cocoa' (exactly 5 letters) passes len(w) > 5 — it does not, because 5 > 5 is False.



If your prediction was exactly right: great, move on. If not: even better — figure out why before continuing, because this loop-plus-conditional shape is the skeleton of the trial loop you will build today.
One more, faster. Predict, then run:
stimuli = ['wheel_L.jpg', 'wheel_R.jpg', 'gear_L.jpg']

for s in stimuli:
    if '_L' in s:
        print(s, '-> left')
    else:
        print(s, '-> right')






Check your prediction





wheel_L.jpg -> left
wheel_R.jpg -> right
gear_L.jpg -> left
'_L' in s asks whether the substring '_L' appears anywhere in the string s. Remember this one — it becomes the heart of the feedback logic in Chapter 9.



That is all the warm-up you need. Next: the screen.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window

title: 10 · Exercise 5: Responses and Feedback
text:
Block 4 milestone · Exercise 5 running by ~15:30; advanced tasks if time
Make a copy of your Exercise 4 script first (e.g. cogwheel_v2.py). Session 3 wants the original too. Then upgrade it in four steps, running after each.

title: 10 · Exercise 5: Responses and Feedback
text:
Advanced (pick any, in any order)
A. Keep score. Count correct answers; report the score in the goodbye message using an f-string.






Show the code





# before the loop:
n_correct = 0

# in the correct-answer branch:
n_correct = n_correct + 1

# goodbye message:
goodbye = visual.TextStim(win,
    text=f'You got {n_correct} out of {len(images)} correct. Thank you!',
    color='white')



B. Add sounds. Play a sound on correct answers.






Show the code





from psychopy import sound

# once, before the loop:
correct_sound = sound.Sound('correct.wav')

# in the correct-answer branch:
correct_sound.play()



C. Write a reusable function. The prepare–draw–flip–wait pattern repeats constantly — exactly what functions are for. Write show_image() and use it in your loop.






Show the code





def show_image(win, image_path, keyList=None):
    stim = visual.ImageStim(win, image=image_path)
    stim.draw()
    win.flip()
    keys = event.waitKeys(keyList=keyList)
    return keys[0]

# the trial loop becomes wonderfully short:
for image in images:
    key = show_image(win, image, keyList=['left', 'right'])
    ...

title: Session 2: Introduction to PsychoPy
text: Welcome back! In Session 1 you learned to think in Python: variables, lists, loops, conditionals, and functions. That is all we need to program sophisticated experiments. For this session, we are going to work in the PsychoPy Coder on your own laptop. By the end of today, you will have built a working experiment that shows images in random order, collects keyboard responses, and gives feedback on every trial. Today, we change environment.

title: Session 2: Introduction to PsychoPy
text:
Learning outcomes
After this session, you can:

Open and close a PsychoPy window and explain the draw–flip cycle (prepare, draw, flip) that gives experiments their precise timing.
Present text and image stimuli (TextStim, ImageStim), for a fixed duration (core.wait()) or until a keypress (event.waitKeys()).
Load stimulus files dynamically with glob.glob() instead of hardcoding filenames.
Randomise trial order with random.shuffle() and explain why randomisation matters.
Collect and restrict keyboard responses (keyList=['left','right']) and use the response in your code.
Give conditional feedback: evaluate a response against a rule and show a success or failure image.


How today works
Today alternates between two modes. In short lecture segments we introduce each concept and demonstrate it live on the projector; in the exercises you put the concepts to work on your own, at your own pace, with the teaching team circulating. The chapters on this site follow the same order as the lectures, so everything shown at the front is here to re-read.

title: 8 · Collecting Keyboard Responses
text:
Block 3 · aim to finish chapters 7-9 by the afternoon break (~14:15)
So far, any key advances the experiment. For a real task we want a specific response (i.e., left or right arrow), and we want to know which one was pressed. Both jobs are done by the keyList argument:

title: 8 · Collecting Keyboard Responses
text:
Try it
In a scratch script (or your experiment), show one image and collect a left/right response for it, printing the key to the console.






Show the code





img = visual.ImageStim(win, image=images[0])
img.draw()
win.flip()

keys = event.waitKeys(keyList=['left', 'right'])
key = keys[0]
print('Response was:', key)









Tip: a polite emergency exit



Add 'escape' to your keyList and handle it: if key == 'escape': win.close(); core.quit(). Very handy in fullscreen experiments.

title: 9 · Conditional Feedback
text:
Block 3 · aim to finish chapters 7-9 by the afternoon break (~14:15)

To give feedback we must know whether a response was correct, but “correct” is not something the computer knows by itself. We have to operationalise it: define a rule, in code, that maps stimulus properties onto expected responses. In the CogWheel experiment, that rule lives in the filenames: images ending in _L.jpg require a left response, _R.jpg a right response.
You already met the tool for reading that rule in Chapter 1: the substring check.
# derive the correct answer from the stimulus filename
if '_L' in image:
    correct_key = 'left'
else:
    correct_key = 'right'

# compare the response to the correct answer
if key == correct_key:
    feedback = visual.ImageStim(win, image='success.jpg')
else:
    feedback = visual.ImageStim(win, image='failure.jpg')

feedback.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(2)     # show the feedback for exactly 2 seconds
Notice the structure: two small decisions rather than one big one. The first if-block derives the correct answer from the stimulus; the second compares it to the response. Splitting logic like this is good style — and much easier to debug.






🔮 Predict first




What does '_L' in 'stimuli/stimulus7_L.jpg' evaluate to? (b) Why core.wait(2) rather than event.waitKeys() for feedback? (c) Why does the feedback need its own draw() and flip() when we already flipped for the stimulus?







Check your prediction






True. (b) Feedback should be a fixed, brief event, identical for everyone and not something to sit on or skip. (c) Every new screen needs its own draw-flip: the stimulus flip put the cogwheel on stage; replacing it with feedback means drawing backstage and raising the curtain again.






This is the last piece you need. On to the main exercise of the day.

title: 7 · Randomising Trial Order
text:
Block 3 · aim to finish chapters 7-9 by the afternoon break (~14:15)

Right now every participant sees the stimuli in the same order. That is a problem: people get better with practice, tired with time, bored towards the end. With a fixed order these order effects are confounded with the stimuli themselves. Stimulus 1 always meets a fresh participant, stimulus 20 a weary one. The simplest fix: give every participant a different random order, so order effects average out.






🔮 Predict first



A fellow student writes this. What happens when it runs?
import random

images = ['stim1_L.jpg', 'stim2_R.jpg', 'stim3_L.jpg']
images = random.shuffle(images)

for image in images:
    print(image)






Check your prediction





It crashes: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable. random.shuffle() reorders the list in place and returns None, so the assignment replaced the list with None, and the loop had nothing to iterate over. This is today’s most classic gotcha. The fix:
random.shuffle(images)   # its own line: no assignment!





The correct pattern, which you should now add to your Exercise 4 script (right after the glob line):
import random

images = glob.glob('stimuli/stimulus*.jpg')
random.shuffle(images)   # shuffles IN PLACE
Run your experiment twice. You should get two different orders. That’s randomisation working.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text: Welcome! Over the coming workshop sessions, you’ll go from typing your very first line of Python to watching a full behavioural experiment run on your own screen: window, stimuli, responses, feedback, the lot. Between you and that moment stand a handful of Python concepts and a few dozen extremely fixable error messages. We assume no programming experience. If you can rename a file, you’re qualified to start.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why programming?
Nearly every empirical experiment in cognitive science — reaction-time studies, reading paradigms, eye-tracking, EEG — is implemented in code. A working knowledge of Python allows you to build precisely the experiment your research question requires, to understand the structure and provenance of your data, and to diagnose problems when they arise.
The aim of these three sessions is a modest form of fluency: by the end, the experiment running on your screen should be a system you can read, modify, and reason about. These skills will hopefully outlast the course: designing, implementing, and troubleshooting your own experiments is part of the everyday craft of working scientists, in cognitive science and well beyond.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why Python and not R?
The Python programming language is optimal for coding experiments because it has a special library called PsychoPy for doing so.
In contrast, the R programming language is optimal for statistical analyses, as it was designed specifically for this purpose.
Therefore, this workshop on programming for experiments focuses on Python instead of R, which you instead cover in your Methods 1 practical classes.
However, as you will learn over the course of the semester, many of the programming concepts that we cover in Session 1 are generalizable to R and all other languages.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
The three sessions
Session 1 · Python basics Variables, lists, loops, conditionals, functions. These are the handful of building blocks that all programs are made of. Everything you learn here gets used directly in Session 2.
Session 2 · Introduction to PsychoPy PsychoPy is the Python library psychologists use to run experiments: it opens windows, draws stimuli, and records keypresses with precise timing. You build the CogWheel experiment step by step and leave with a script that runs: images in random order, keyboard responses, feedback on every trial, and more..
Session 3 · From cogwheels to words (materials coming) Swap the images for words, add a clock and a logfile, and your CogWheel script becomes a self-paced reading experiment, the direct starting point for your Portfolio 2 prototype.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
How the sessions work
Each session follows the same rhythm: a short lecture introduces the concepts and demonstrates them live, and you then put them to work in a set of exercises you complete on your own, at your own pace, with the teaching team circulating. Three habits will serve you well throughout:

Predict before you run. Whenever you see a 🔮 Predict first box, write down what the code will do before running it.
Run constantly. Run your code after every small change, not after twenty lines. Small steps make bugs easy to find.
Never stay stuck. Ten minutes on the same bug is the signal to ask: check the error message, unfold the solution, or wave a teacher over. Sitting silently with a bug is the one wrong way to use these sessions.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
What you need

Your own laptop with PsychoPy installed. Install instructions are sent out before Session 1, and each session starts with a setup check. If the install fights back, come 15 minutes early.
Curiosity. A willingness to try things, break things, and read the occasional error message will carry you further than any prior experience would.

Ready? Start with Session 1.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text: Block 2 · Chapter 2 of 3 before the first break. Understand what a variable is in Python & the different types of variables.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
What is a variable?
A variable is a name we give to a value so we can store it and use it later in our code. The name stays the same, but the value stored in it can change while the program is running. A variable can store a number, a word, or a list of values.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Your first variable
Let’s create our first variable in Python. We will call it my_name and store a name in it.
my_name = "anna"
We can also add comments to explain what our code is doing. In Python, a comment starts with #. Everything after # on that line is ignored by Python.
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"
Now run the code by selecting it in your file and pressing Shift+Enter.
You will see the code executed in the console below. If you then type my_name on a new line and press Enter, Python will print the value stored in the variable:
>>> my_name = 'anna'
>>> my_name
'anna'
An easier way to see the output is to use the print() function:
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"

# This line prints the value stored in my_name.
print(my_name)
Select these lines and press Shift+Enter. You should see the value of my_name appear in the console.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Variable types
Python allows us to create variables that store different kinds of data. Today we will focus on some of the most common variable types.
We can find the type of a variable by using the type() function:
# Query the type of my_name.
type(my_name)
This returns <class 'str'>, which means that my_name is a string variable.

title: Exercise 2 · Lists
text:
Block 3 · Learning goals: Understand what a list is and how to use them effectively.







Defining lists





Make variables containing 10-item lists. Make one of each list below:
 1. All character items

 2. All integer items

 3. All floating point numeric items

 4. Mixed character, floating point and integer items. 
Now combine lists 1-3 in a single long list.









Indexing lists





Return the 4th item in each of lists 1-3.
Return the first item in the list of lists (the combined list you made above).
Do you notice anything unexpected about the output?
Can you figure out how to index the first word only in the combined list?









Changing list items





Okay, now let’s take advantage of list mutability by changing our lists.

Replace a list item with another (using indexing) in one of your lists.
Append an item to the end of one of your lists list.
Insert a new item into a list between two existing items.
Replace the first list item in your combined list with a new item.

title: 3 · Lists
text: Block 2 · Learning goals: Understand what a list is and how to use lists effectively.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
What are lists?
Lists = literally a list of “elements” that can be changed (are mutable).
How to define lists?

Variable name = [ item1, item2, item3…itemN ]

Lists can contain items of the same type and different types.






Make some lists





You can create lists with all strings, all numeric data, or a combination, see below.

# first simple lists of same type items.
shopping = [ "apples", "pears", "bananas" ] 
test_scores = [ 90, 60, 100, 82]

# now mixed items.
mixed_list = [ "cats", 7, 309.45 ]
You can print lists as below.

print(test_scores)
print(mixed_list)
You can also combine lists.

# now lists of lists!
combined = [ shopping, test_scores, mixed_list ]









Indexing lists





We can also index lists (just like we indexed character strings), i.e., by using the square brackets after the list name, and putting the index inside of the square brackets. See below.

# Let's index our lists!

print(shopping[0])
print(shopping[1])
print(shopping[2])

# Sub-indexing. What does the below return?
print(shopping[0][0:2])
You may recognize the above syntax for indexing lists from the previous learning block.
If you do, that’s because we were already working with lists when we used the .split method for character strings. Splitting a character string by a delimiter such as a space returns a list, where each item is a string of characters that were not separated by the delimiter.









Changing list items





Lists are mutable, meaning that we can change their items. For example, you can:

Replace a list item with another (using indexing)
Append an item to the end of a list.
Insert a new item into a list between two existing items.


# Here is our original list. 
print(shopping)

# And now let's replace the second list item with "kiwi"
shopping[1] = "kiwi"

# Let's print our mutated list.
print(shopping)

# Now let's add an item to our list. 
shopping.append("raspberry")

# Let's print our elaborated list.
print(shopping)

# We can also add an item by inserting it at a particular location in the list.
shopping.insert(1, "blueberry")

# Let's look at our further mutated list. 
print(shopping)

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 1: Regular string variables
String variables are defined by strings of characters. String variables are specified using single or double quotation marks around the string.
# If you use single quotes here, it won't work. Why?
dog_name_possessive = 'anna's dog's name is..'

# If you use double-quotes here it will work. 
dog_name_possessive = "anna's dog's name is.."






🤔 Think first



Why does the single-quoted version fail while the double-quoted version works?






Check your thinking





The apostrophe in anna’s ends the single-quoted string early. Python thinks the string stops after anna, and the rest is nonsense to it. Double quotes let Python see the apostrophe as just another character inside the string.






Indexing
Strings are stored like arrays of characters, meaning that you can individually access single characters in the string using indexing (square brackets around the indices you want to extract).
# Here you are indexing the first 4 characters in the variable my_name_possessive. 
# You use square brackets around the indices that you want to extract.
dog_name_possessive[0:4] # extract 4 characters from the 0th character.

# you can also count backwards from the end of a string using the minus sign, e.g.:
dog_name_possessive[-4:]
You may have noticed that we start indexing at 0 instead of 1. This is because Python is a zero-indexed language, so whenever you have a multi-item variable, the first item is always indexed using 0 instead of 1. CAREFUL: R is a 1-indexed langauge, so you always index the first item in a multi-item variable using 1 in R instead of 0.

Before you run it: what will dog_name_possessive[0:4] give you?

anna — characters 0, 1, 2 and 3. The index range [0:4] starts at 0 and stops before 4, so you get exactly 4 characters. (The console shows it wrapped in quotes — 'anna' — because it is a string.)


:::

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
String methods
String variables have many built-in methods that we can call on them. Here are some useful string methods:

split()
If you type the name of your string variable followed by .split(), Python splits the string into smaller pieces, using the space character as the default delimiter. Try it in the console:
dog_name_possessive.split()
>>> ["anna's", "dog's", 'name', 'is..']
The split() method returns a list of strings. Each item is one part of the original text, separated by the chosen delimiter.
You can store the output in a variable, and since it is a list, you can index it, even down to characters within each item:
split_variable = dog_name_possessive.split()
split_variable[0]
split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> split_variable[0]
>>> "anna's"
>>> split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
>>> 'a'
>>> split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> 'o'
So split_variable[1][1] means: take item 1 of the list ("dog's": remember, zero-indexed!), then character 1 of that string.
You can also use split() with a different delimiter, such as an underscore:
subject_id = "S_01"
subject_id.split("_")
['S', '01']

Given responses = "left right left left", what does responses.split() return?

['left', 'right', 'left', 'left']: a list of four strings, one per word. Repeats are kept; split() just cuts, it doesn’t deduplicate.



Given date = "2026-09-14", what does date.split("-") return?

The delimiter is the cut line — it doesn’t survive into the pieces.


['2026', '09', '14']. Three pieces, dashes gone. Note they are strings, not numbers: '09' keeps its leading zero, and you couldn’t do maths with it without converting first.




upper()
The upper() method converts all letters in a string to uppercase.
name = "anna"
name.upper()
>>> 'ANNA'
Note that upper() does not change name itself — it returns a new, uppercased string. If you want to keep it, store it:
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
>>> ANNA
# or store the result in a new variable.
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
Here are a few more useful string methods:
word = " subject_01 "
print(word.lower())
print(word.strip())
print(word.replace("p", "P"))
print(word.startswith(" "))
print(word.endswith(" "))


len()
And, finally, we can get the length of a string variable using len() (not a string-specific method)
len(word)
>>> 12
The 10 characters of subject_01 plus the two spaces. Invisible characters count, which is exactly why .strip() exists.
There’s lots more that you can do with strings, but these are the basics!

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 2: Regular numeric variables
Now let’s turn to our other fundamental variable type: numeric. There are two basic numeric types:

Integers: whole numbers (no decimal point)
Floating points: numbers with a decimal point

# This is an integer.
a = 1
type(a)
>>> int
# This is a floating point.
b = 1.5
type(b)
>>> float
c = 1.00

c stores the value one, but what does type(c) return? float or int?

<class 'float'>: a floating point. The value is a whole number, but writing it with a decimal point makes it a float. What matters is how it is written, not what it equals.


The same logic applies to operations:
# What happens when you combine types in operations?
d = b + c
type(d)
>>> float
Adding the float b to the float c gives a float — d is 2.5. And even when an operation on two floats produces a whole number, the result stays a floating point:
e = 1.5 + 1.5
type(e)
print(e)
<class 'float'>
3.0
The value is three — but Python shows it as 3.0: the .0 is the float’s badge. It never silently becomes an integer.
Standard numeric operations are addition (shown above), subtraction, multiplication and division:
print(a - b)   # subtraction
print(a * b)   # multiplication
print(a / b)   # division
-0.5
1.5
0.6666666666666666

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Printing variables with f-strings
Imagine that you want to print reaction times for a given subject on an experiment screen. The subject is different in each experiment, and so is their reaction time.
You can create a special expression called an f-string, where you embed variables inside a string: start the string with f, then place variable names inside curly brackets {}.
subject_id = "S_01"
reaction_time = 0.45
message = f"Reaction time for {subject_id}: {reaction_time:.2f} seconds"
Here {subject_id} inserts the value of the subject ID variable, and {reaction_time:.2f} inserts the value of reaction_time, where .2f formats the number with two digits after the decimal point.

What exactly does print(message) show?

Reaction time for S_01: 0.45 seconds: the curly-bracket parts are replaced by the variables’ values, and everything else is printed as-is. In Session 2, messages like this become the text you show on the experiment screen.


All predictions checked? Next: Exercise 1a — Variables & data types.

Print the string "Null hypothesis: Eating ice cream does not improve mood".

title: Exercise 1a: Variables & variable types
text:
Part 3: String methods

Split null_hypothesis by spaces and store the output in a variable called split_var.
Print split_var[1]. What is the output? What is the function of the square brackets, and of the index inside them?
Print the second character of split_var[1].
Split null_hypothesis by the colon (:) character and store the output in a new variable.
Index the word 'hypothesis' out of split_var and store it in a variable called hypothesis_word. Look closely at what you get.
Convert hypothesis_word to upper case and store it in hypothesis_word_upper.
Use .replace() to replace the word hypothesis in null_hypothesis with hypothesis_word_upper.
Test whether hypothesis_word_upper starts with "H".
Get the length of null_hypothesis.







Hint





Tasks 2–3: one pair of brackets picks an item from the list; a second pair picks a character from that string. Task 5: split() cut on spaces, so what happened to the colon that had no space before it? Task 7: .replace() wants two things: what to find, and what to put there.









Show the code

print(split_var[1])            # hypothesis: — note the colon came along!
print(split_var[1][1])         # y
split_by_colon = null_hypothesis.split(":")

print(len(null_hypothesis))                       # 55

title: Exercise 1a: Variables & variable types
text:
Part 4: Numbers

Make an integer variable and a floating-point variable.
Print the types of both.
Add them. What type is the result?
Subtract them. What happens?
Divide them.
Multiply them and store the output in a new variable.







Show the code

mean_rt = 0.45
print(type(n_trials), type(mean_rt))
print(n_trials + mean_rt)    # 20.45 — int + float gives float
print(n_trials - mean_rt)

product = n_trials * mean_rt

title: Exercise 1a: Variables & variable types
text:
Part 5: f-strings
Imagine printing information about the current subject on an experiment screen. The subject differs in each experiment, and so does their reaction time.

Make a variable with a subject ID and one with a reaction time.

Show the code
